title: Lior and the Aftermath
premise: Marguerite Eastwick, a translator who has spent decades erasing himself between languages, finds a box of undelivered letters behind his late mother's wardrobe—letters in a dying childhood dialect, written by a man she loved and never mentioned. As the city schedules the demolition of the house where he grew up, Marguerite traces the letter-writer's descendants and uncovers an old injustice: his mother's testimony sent an innocent man to prison to protect her family's name. To finish translating the final untranslatable sentence—a confession he must deliver aloud—he must choose between the duty of silence he inherited and the justice of being seen, ending with him reading the sentence at the demolition site as the walls come down.
about_author: B. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent fifteen years listening to other people's confessions before writing any of their own. They live near a coastline that keeps changing its name, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Marguerite, who works a translation job smoothing over a hostile deposition and returns to his mother's sealed house, practicing his conversation-ending smile on neighbors. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of invisibility established.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing the house before demolition, Marguerite pries loose a panel and finds a shoebox of letters in Vessic, the childhood dialect he half-remembers. POV: Marguerite. Beat: wonder curdling into dread as he recognizes his mother's handwriting on the envelopes' return address.

chapters.title: A Language of Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Marguerite's memory-voice: how Vessic was beaten out of him at school, word by word, until only nouns remained. He begins cataloguing what he's lost. Beat: grief for a language treated like a wound.

chapters.title: The First Letter
chapters.summary: Marguerite translates the earliest letter slowly, using an old dictionary, learning the writer—Tomas—was his mother's lover. POV: Marguerite interwoven with Tomas's epistolary voice. Beat: intimacy with strangers across time.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The city posts the official date: six weeks. A neighbor, Odile, urges him to fight it; he declines with his practiced smile. Beat: duty versus desire introduced—the house as both prison and last witness.

chapters.title: What Mother Never Said
chapters.summary: Reading further, Marguerite learns Tomas was arrested weeks after the letters stopped—and that his mother testified against him. POV: Marguerite, with a chilling courtroom fragment from her diary tucked among the letters. Beat: betrayal discovered in the family archive.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: Marguerite visits a municipal records office and meets Sef, a young archivist who helps him pull trial files and treats his broken Vessic as precious rather than shameful. Beat: first warmth; the possibility of being known.

chapters.title: Prisoner 4471
chapters.summary: The file reveals Tomas served eleven years for arson he likely didn't commit; the fire destroyed a rival family's warehouse. Marguerite realizes his grandfather's business benefited. Beat: inherited guilt, justice outside the law taking shape.

chapters.title: Odile's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Odile, who knew his mother, feeds him soup and half-truths, revealing the family paid witnesses. She warns him: some doors open onto rooms you can't leave. Beat: complicity of the whole neighborhood exposed.

chapters.title: Translating the Untranslatable
chapters.summary: Marguerite reaches the final letter, whose closing sentence resists every dictionary—Tomas's forgiveness or accusation, grammatically both. He obsesses over it nightly. Beat: the central metaphor crystallized; love against duty made linguistic.

chapters.title: Sef's Question
chapters.summary: Over late hours in the archive, Sef asks why Marguerite hides behind translation instead of speaking. A near-kiss interrupted by his reflexive smile. Beat: romance kindled and immediately defended against.

chapters.title: The Grandfather's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic, Marguerite finds ledgers proving payments to two witnesses, including his own godfather, still alive in a care home. Beat: rising tension—the living can be confronted, and will lie.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts the godfather, who neither confirms nor denies but says, 'Your mother carried it so you wouldn't have to.' Beat: duty's true face—not honor, but a burden passed down.

chapters.title: The Descendant
chapters.summary: Marguerite locates Tomas's granddaughter, Lena, a carpenter restoring houses slated for demolition. She is furious that a stranger arrives bearing old wounds. Beat: hope rejected; the cost of showing up uninvited.

chapters.title: Letters Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Lena relents when Marguerite reads one letter aloud in his fractured Vessic; hearing the language spoken moves her more than the content. Beat: reconciliation through voice, not argument.

chapters.title: Petition Denied
chapters.summary: Together they petition to stay the demolition pending historical review; the city refuses—no landmark status, no standing. Beat: legal justice fails; the clock accelerates.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Again
chapters.summary: Marguerite finally parses the untranslatable line: it forgives his mother conditionally—forgiveness contingent on truth being told. He understands he is the condition. Beat: climax approaching; the personal stakes named.

chapters.title: Confession at the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Marguerite confesses to Sef everything his family did and his own years of silence; Sef listens without absolving him, then stays anyway. Beat: love chosen over safety; the smile finally fails him.

chapters.title: What the Witnesses Owe
chapters.summary: Marguerite delivers the ledger evidence to a journalist and to Lena, knowing it will shame his dead mother publicly. The godfather dies quietly the same night. Beat: irreversible act; grief and relief tangled.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: The night before the wrecking crew arrives, Marguerite, Lena, Odile, and Sef hold a wake in the empty house, reading all the letters aloud in turn. Beat: communal mourning; the house becomes a mouth at last.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence, Spoken
chapters.summary: At dawn, before the machines, Marguerite reads Tomas's final sentence aloud in Vessic, then translates it into the language of the present: naming his mother's crime and Tomas's conditional forgiveness fulfilled. Beat: climax—truth spoken, identity claimed.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the article runs; Lena restores a house nearby and teaches Marguerite words he lost; Sef helps him begin translating Vessic children's songs for print. Beat: resolution—justice delivered outside the law, love chosen, a language rebuilt one borrowed word returned.
